Radio signals from outer space are not new,
but they are just as mystifying today
as they were when Marconi first picked them up more than 50 years ago.

Like Marconi, Tesla had no qualms about making a public report on his findings. If Mars was

The signals were recorded by RCA, discussed, then filed and forgotten. But they were suddenly

Scarcely more than a year after the RCA incident, the naval research experts were testing the Jenkins process while recording wireless signals on photographic film.
Out of the ether came a weird chirping that made no sense in terms of intelligible code.
But when the film was developed, the scientists were astounded at the results.
Instead of recording as intermittent dots and dashes, the weird code had arrived in such a fashion that it was recorded in the form of faces.
Rude caricatures, to be sure, but faces beyond a doubt.
In 1926, the United States government financed a project
which was designed to contact Mars by radio, if possible.
Scientists from Johns Hopkins University,
aided by radio experts from both the Navy and the Signal Corps,
selected a spot in Nebraska.
There, they spent hundreds of thousands of dollars
constructing a powerful transmitter and delicate receiving sets.
For two weeks, they sent radio signals in the direction of Mars
and waited, hopefully, for some indication that they had been heard.
The net result, according to the official statement, was inconclusive.
Thirty years later, great observatories all over the world
were installing costly radio telescopes,
huge metallic dishes that can be focused on individual planets.
On June 4, 1956, the Naval Observatory in Washington
in making what it called the first radio contact with Venus,
a contact which led them to believe that Venus had a surface temperature
about equal to that of boiling water.
Ohio State University reported that its radio astronomer, Dr. John Krause,
had used their radio telescope to receive two types of signals,
including the Class II signals, which, said the university,
have many of the characteristics of a terrestrial radio transmitting station.
These signals, which Dr. Krauss said resembled radio telegraphy in many ways, were received only when the giant radio telescope at the university was trained precisely on Venus.

had no difficulty picking up the same signal. Now, freak long-range television pickups are
rather more common than most viewers realize, and the British authorities attached no unusual
significance to the reception of K.L.E.E. until they contacted the Texas station. Then
shock. KLEE went off the air in 1950. The successor to KLEE notified the British that no KLEE

picked up in Britain. The officials in Britain ruled out the possibility that it could have been
a pointless practical joke, which would have cost at least $100,000 to perpetrate. Where did the
the signal come from? Why was it beamed only to the British Isles? The chief engineer for the
